To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the relative calibration of reflected spectral radiances from a single radiometer is best assessed using the linear regression between reflectances at the 0.66- and 0.86-μm wavelengths.

the linear relationships of reflectance with wavelength are remarkably insensitive to the factors governing the reflectances themselves; that the relationships are insensitive to the factors affecting the reflectances; and that the slopes and offsets of these relationships provide useful information about the relative calibration accuracies of the different channels of an imaging radiometer.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a technique that uses sun glint for the relative calibration of imaging radiometers and the assessment of the accuracy of the relative calibrations.
the use of sun glint to calibrate the reflectance of ocean surfaces.
the use of sun glint as a means of checking the relative calibration of reflected spectral radiances.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in the absence of a direct calibration of the radiances of a multispectral radiometer, it is possible to assess the relative calibrations of its different spectral channels by observing sunlight reflected from regions where the surface reflectance is known, or can be assumed, to be constant with wavelength.

, provided that all of the assumptions and conditions are satisfied, the use of sun glint to calibrate imaging radiometers can be very effective, and the method is very useful for checking the relative calibrations of different channels of the same instrument and of different instruments.

the relative calibration of channels is good, with the possible exception of the 0.66-μm channel of the Nimbus 7 Coastal Zone Color Scanner, and that the absolute calibration of the channels is good, within the limits of the accuracy of the solar irradiance measurements and the atmospheric correction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
sun glint can be used to check relative calibration of reflected spectral radiances with a precision of about 2% or better.
we have shown that sun-glint reflectance is an excellent tool for assessing the relative accuracy of the calibration of the different spectral channels of an instrument.
we have demonstrated the utility of sun glint for checking the relative calibrations of reflected radiances, but the technique is still somewhat limited.
The main takeaway from our work is that
sun glint is a very robust method to assess the relative calibrations of reflected spectral radiance measurements from an imaging radiometer.
the relative accuracy of spectral reflectances can be checked using sun glint, provided that the atmosphere is transparent and the solar zenith angles are less than about 30°.
